units.translation: An example of the verb derived from this, ὀπηδέω [to follow], is in the verses falsely attributed to Aeschylus (fr. 284) in Theophilus ad Autol. 2 p. 378a and Stob. Ecl. vol. 1 p. 120
where the form ὀπάζει [he grants] written in Theophilus shows the Attic form ὀπαδεῖ [he follows].
The vision has gone, not later than the winged attendants on the paths of sleep.
They appointed these my attendants and spear-bearing companions.
Sometimes it may be translated as 'to make, to produce', but in such a way that some notion of granting is added.
In addition to these, I granted them fire.
From which Zeus the lord granted this honor.
God granted power to every middle course.
He stole the light of all-crafting fire and granted it to mortals.
What a race of women you granted.
Whoever granted this deed against the shield.
He orders the spear-bearing attendants to lead.
Send attendants and guides of the local people.
by what way or by what means
Thus Dobree for χειροπληθύεται [is filled by hand].
where ὅπη [where] is read from the copies for ὅποι [whither].
I am at a loss, deprived of thought, where to turn my resourceful care (Karsten reads εὐπαλάμων μεριμνᾶν [of resourceful cares]).
The ruling hand of the people, where (i.e. in what direction) it is filled.
For I do not see the plan of Zeus, where I might flee.
There is a way in which it now is.
Soon we shall know where the sign is being fulfilled.
For I do not know where it is being fulfilled.
Nor can I learn where (M has ὅπη [where]) I shall escape troubles.
Thus Wellauer for ὄπισθεν δ᾽ [and from behind].
A spear heavy at the back.
where Hermann rightly, as it seems, reads ὀπισθόπουν τε τοῦδε καὶ ξυνέμπορον [walking behind this man and accompanying him].
Lead him into the hospitable men's halls, and these who walk behind and accompany him.
walking behind this man and accompanying him
The Judgment of Arms was the title of a play by Aeschylus (fr. 172-176).
concerning which passage see under ποτιχρίμπτομαι.
Blamable in the arrangement of arms.
Having fenced their bodies with well-bronzed arms.
with little probability introduced by some into the corrupt passage σπαργανηπλείζετο [was swaddled], where undoubtedly another verb ending in ἱζετο [was seated] is hidden.
The torch blazes, armed in their hands.
Tumults of spears and naval armaments.
It is not fitting for a hoplite to love this word.
Heavy, wrestling in armor, destructive to opponents.
